title: Choosing yarn fibre
subtitle: What the fibre content of a yarn tells you about how it will behave
excerpt: The fibre content of a yarn determines how it blocks, washes, wears, and feels. Wool has memory and blocks beautifully. Cotton is heavy but washable. Acrylic is hard-wearing and cheap. Understanding what each fibre does helps you choose the right yarn for a project before you start.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — yarn selection. Standard crochet and textile reference material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Yarn made from animal sources: wool, alpaca, cashmere, mohair, silk. Protein fibres block with steam or water, have natural elasticity, and are warm. Most are not machine washable unless labelled superwash.
Yarn made from plant sources: cotton, linen, bamboo, hemp. Cellulose fibres have little elasticity, are usually washable, and become softer and more drapey over time and washes.

content.text: Yarn fibres split broadly into
protein fibres
(animal),
cellulose fibres
(plant), and synthetics (acrylic, polyester, nylon). Each group behaves differently in the hook, in blocking, and in wear.
Wool and wool-type fibres
Has natural elasticity — the yarn bounces back, which makes consistent tension easier.
Blocks beautifully with steam or water. Lace and openwork patterns designed for wool open up significantly.
Most are hand wash or dry clean only unless labelled superwash.
Can felt if washed in hot water with agitation — a risk and a design option.
Cotton and plant fibres
No elasticity — the yarn doesn't spring back, which makes uneven tension more visible.
Machine washable at cool temperatures. Ideal for dishcloths, market bags, summer garments.
Heavier than wool for the same weight category — a large cotton blanket is noticeably heavier than a wool one.
Shows stitch definition clearly — good for textured patterns.
Acrylic and synthetic fibres
Machine washable at most temperatures. Practical for children's items and anything that will be washed frequently.
Doesn't block with water — needs steam heat to relax. Or simply steam-blocking to set shape permanently.
Hard-wearing: doesn't pill as quickly as some wools, doesn't felt.
Cheap to buy in large quantities — practical for first-project practice.
